summary: Specifies how the MEID URN can serve as an Instance ID, an identifier used to tell apart instances of a device or service, using the 3GPP2 URN namespace.

eli5.summary: A phone's ID number can also be used as the name tag for that particular phone in other systems.

questions: what is a meid instance id
subtitle: Using mobile device IDs as unique identifiers in SIP networks.

tldr.problem: 3GPP2 mobile devices need a way to be identified in SIP/IMS voice networks while also supporting fallback to circuit-switched networks. A single, globally unique identifier that works across both domains is needed.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how the MEID (Mobile Equipment Identity), a globally unique phone hardware identifier, can be formatted as a URN and used as an Instance ID in the SIP +sip.instance parameter, allowing SIP registrars and servers to recognize and track individual phone devices.
tldr.outcome: Mobile carriers can now use MEID URNs to identify specific phones during emergency services, equipment verification, and handover between IP and circuit-switched calls. This RFC links to RFC 8464, which defines how to format the MEID as a URN.

today: RFC 8465 is an Informational RFC published in September 2018 and remains the definition of how 3GPP2 mobile devices use MEID as a SIP Instance ID. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Phones Need a Unique Network ID
sections.content: This RFC shows how a phone's built-in hardware identifier, called a MEID (Mobile Equipment Identity), can be used as a unique device ID in SIP networks. The MEID is globally unique, assigned by 3GPP2 standards bodies, and all 3GPP2 phones already have one. The key insight is that as 3GPP2 networks transition from pure circuit-switched voice to IP-based calling, a phone may have two network domains active at once: an IP/SIP domain and a circuit-switched domain. The MEID is the only identifier that bridges both worlds and travels through both signaling paths.
sections.eli5: When your phone switches between internet calling and regular cellular calls in the middle of a conversation, the network needs one ID that both systems understand.

sections.title: The Migration Challenge
sections.content: 3GPP2 networks evolved from circuit-switched systems to support IP-based IMS (IP Multimedia Subsystem) with SIP. During the transition, many phones operate in both modes: they can take calls via IP and via circuit-switched radio. To move a call between these domains without dropping it, a Mobile Switching Center (MSC) server coordinates the switch. It receives SIP signaling from the IP side and circuit-switched signaling from the radio side. To ensure the call belongs to the same phone, the MSC server needs an identifier visible in both domains. The MEID meets this requirement: it is encoded in both circuit-switched signaling and, with this RFC, in SIP messages.
sections.eli5: Imagine switching between wifi calling and cell signal—the network needs one phone ID that works in both places to keep your call going.

sections.title: Three Key Use Cases
sections.content: First, phones send their MEID in SIP REGISTER messages so the network can check an Equipment Identity Register (EIR) to verify the phone is not stolen and allowed on the network. Stolen phones can be blocked immediately. Second, during emergency calls, phones include their MEID so that a Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) can identify the phone if the caller is unable to speak or the SIM is absent. Third, when an emergency session handed over from the IP domain to circuit-switched, the MEID is the common link: the Emergency Access Transfer Function can match the circuit call to the SIP session using the MEID, ensuring continuity.
sections.eli5: The network uses MEID to block stolen phones, to know which phone calls when you cannot speak, and to keep emergency calls alive when switching networks mid-call.

sections.title: How It Works in Practice
sections.content: When a 3GPP2 phone registers with an IMS network, it includes its MEID URN in the +sip.instance Contact header parameter, formatted according to RFC 8464. A SIP registrar receiving this MEID URN follows the procedures of RFC 5626 to track that contact as belonging to a specific device instance, allowing multiple registrations (from different network paths or locations) to be recognized as the same phone. If the registrar supports GRUUs (Globally Routable User Agent URIs per RFC 5627), it must obfuscate the MEID in the public GRUU to prevent exposing the device ID. A phone MUST NOT send its MEID in routine non-REGISTER requests, only in REGISTER and emergency-related messages, to protect privacy. A User Agent Server (UAS) likewise MUST NOT send MEID in response Contact headers except for emergency sessions.
sections.eli5: The phone tells the network its ID when signing in or during emergencies, but keeps quiet about its ID for routine calls to stay private.
